variants.name: AsyncStream with an explicit buffering policy
variants.implementation_notes: Swift's structured-concurrency answer is AsyncStream with an explicit buffering policy: .bufferingNewest(n) keeps the newest n elements and drops the oldest, .bufferingOldest(n) keeps the oldest and drops the newest, and the default (when no policy is given) is .unbounded - the failure mode the pattern prevents. yield returns a YieldResult whose .dropped(value) tells the producer that data was lost, and consumption via `for await` is pull-based, so a custom AsyncSequence can implement true demand-driven backpressure by suspending next() until work exists. The classic bounded-queue structure is replaced by the stream's own buffer plus this policy, and onTermination is where cancellation cleanup belongs.
pitfalls: Omitting bufferingPolicy selects .unbounded, and an unbounded AsyncStream terminates with every element it accumulated.
yield's .dropped result must be handled: ignoring it turns the chosen policy into silent data loss.
.bufferingOldest drops the newest elements (the ones just produced), so it is not a latest-wins policy.
A producer that keeps yielding after finish() does nothing visible; termination must be coordinated through onTermination.

variants.name: Combine demand and bounded buffers (Apple platforms)
variants.implementation_notes: On Apple platforms Combine encodes demand explicitly: a Subscriber declares a Subscribers.Demand (max(n), none, or unlimited) and publishers honour it, so flatMap(maxPublishers:) bounds the number of upstream subscriptions and the bounded buffer operator makes one explicit queue whose whenFull policy decides between dropping and failing. The classic queue is replaced by the demand integer travelling through the subscription chain. Demand is per-subscription and cannot be propagated to a non-cooperative publisher, and Demand.unlimited is a request for the source's full speed, so Combine's protection stops exactly where a source ignores demand.
pitfalls: Demand.unlimited publishes as fast as the source can produce, which is exactly the unprotected case.
A Combine buffer's whenFull drop policies are lossy by design; only failing (or requesting less) preserves every value.
Combine is Apple-platform only and not available with the core Swift concurrency runtime, so a portable choice is AsyncStream.
Each publisher in a chain must honour demand; a custom Publisher that emits regardless breaks the contract for everything downstream.
